Yasser Arafat. The founder and longtime leader of the Palestine Liberation Organization and the principal architect of Palestinian nationalism as a political movement. Arafat founded the Fatah faction in nineteen fifty-nine, an armed nationalist movement, and became chairman of the Palestine Liberation Organization, or PLO, in nineteen sixty-nine. He led the PLO's guerrilla campaign against Israel from the nineteen-sixties through the nineteen-eighties, operating from bases in Jordan, Lebanon, and Tunisia. He was expelled from Jordan between nineteen seventy and nineteen seventy-one, then from Lebanon after the nineteen eighty-two Israeli invasion, after which he relocated the PLO to Tunis. In nineteen ninety-three, Arafat signed the Oslo Accords with Israeli Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin, recognizing Israel and accepting limited Palestinian self-governance in the West Bank and Gaza. He became president of the Palestinian National Authority from nineteen ninety-six to two thousand four, the elected leadership of Palestinian territories. He remained a polarizing figure: to supporters, a nationalist freedom fighter; to critics, complicit in terrorism and corruption. He died in Paris in November two thousand four amid the Second Intifada. His legacy shapes Palestinian political identity to this day, making him the defining face of the Palestinian cause in the broader Arab-Israeli conflict, where Israel remained his ultimate interlocutor and rival.
